sections.title: The flavor comes from your state
The theme comes from your life

toc.title: Thoughts are a clue to your state

blocks.p: I think your thinking is keeping you stuck, and I think you should be doing more feeling. Let's look at what thoughts are, where they come from, and how to use them to get to what you're feeling.

This is a tough question, so we'll keep it general. To me, thoughts are basically words and images in your brain. That could be memories, beliefs, or reasoning. So, words, but also mental functions like reasoning.
I honestly don't think we have much control over what pops into or out of our mind. It feels like we do, but I don't really know if we do. Things just pop in without us directing them.

For example: two plus two equals... There's a good chance the number four popped into your mind, either the image of it or the sound of "four." You didn't choose that. Your brain just populated it on its own.
That's a key piece of what thoughts are: words, images, or sounds that pop in and out of our mind without our conscious direction.
You may know the concept of story follows state, from Deb Dana. Your thoughts come from your polyvagal state. That's a big piece of it, but it's not the full picture, so I want to refine it a bit.

blocks.h3: The flavor comes from your state

blocks.p: The flavor of your thoughts, and their intensity, comes from your polyvagal state. If you're in a fight state, the flavor of your thoughts is going to be more aggressive, more blaming. That doesn't dictate the exact story that comes out. Just the flavor.

blocks.h3: The theme comes from your life

blocks.p: The story itself, the theme of your thoughts, comes from other things: culture, family, social norms, religious views. A lot of it could be what your family in particular passes on to you.

These sources tell you how the world is, how your family is, and how you are, and they can be extremely limiting. Social norms for your gender, for example, about what you're allowed to accomplish, or even what you're allowed to feel. That can be extremely limiting, and it can help keep you stuck.
Deb Dana put it simply when she was on the podcast: "I think we have a theme to our dysregulated stories." ([Episode 29](https://player.captivate.fm/episode/f8b9643c-28f8-4185-9525-8b4e6301516c))

For me, one of the themes in my family growing up, and probably still now, was that we have less. We have less than others. That doesn't need to be true, but it was a belief we had, and it was passed on to me and my siblings: we just have less, and that's how it is.

That stuck with me. Even now, I think that theme is still with me. It isn't a hard and fast truth of life. It's a limiting belief, a theme that was passed on to me. What it sounds like changes with the state I'm in, but the theme is still there: having less, never being able to achieve as much as somebody else, at least financially.
So these themes connect to polyvagal states, the defensive ones and even the safety state.

ul: Shutdown: if it's true that others have more than my family and me, then there's no point in trying. That's very much a shutdown flavor. There's just no point. It's empty. It lacks motivation. There's no energy in it.
Fight: the same theme might sound like jealousy or resentment. "They didn't earn it. It was given to them. How dare they."

Safety: from the safety state, there's more potential to connect with others. If I come to the theme of what can be accomplished in life from safety, I may be more willing and able to connect and collaborate with others to build something together, rather than trying to take other people down and build myself up, or being resentful of what others have.

blocks.p: The thought is different, the flavor is different, but the theme is still there. In the defensive states, the theme reinforces how much I think I can achieve, financially in my case. It's a limiting belief that helps keep me stuck wherever I'm at in life, and that includes stuck in my potential to climb my polyvagal ladder.

And it's not just me. The themes and beliefs given to us can keep any of us down our polyvagal ladder, and limit the potential to climb it and experience more energy, more motivation, more success, more happiness, more connection. If the world is a certain way and there's nothing we can do to change it, the potential to climb our ladders and have different experiences is probably going to be lower.

From the safety state, I'm arguing there's more potential to get unstuck: to try new things, to connect with others, to build a network, or whatever that looks like for you. There's an expansion of possibilities from your safety state. That's when the potential to change your thoughts, to look at the themes of your life and come at them a different way, really changes.

blocks.h: Thoughts are a clue to your state

blocks.p: You probably know you need to feel more. You've heard it from all kinds of wellness people: feel your feelings. It's not easy, though. But let's stick with thoughts for a minute more, because thoughts are a clue to your state.

A thought doesn't just exist on its own. It pops into your mind without you summoning it, but it's driven by something. Its flavor is driven by your state. Its theme probably comes from other sources, from growing up. So here's how to follow a thought down to what's driving it:

ol: Catch the thought. Notice it. That's not easy. Don't exactly question it. Just be curious about it, notice it, and take a look at it. "There's a theme that comes up in my life a lot."
Notice the feeling driving it. Ask, "How do I feel right now?" There's a feeling driving that thought. That's a lot in and of itself.

Notice the state driving the feeling. Feelings don't exist on their own either. They're driven by polyvagal states. And the way you notice your polyvagal state is by experiencing the somatic sensations that come along with it.

blocks.p: If you can do that mindfully, it can help shift your polyvagal state up the ladder.
This is hard to do on your own. A coach or a therapist can be a really good source, another person who can catch these thoughts and themes as they pop up.

In all honesty, feelings can be scary and intimidating. I think all of us struggle with this, but you in particular may not be used to feeling. You may be ignoring, stuffing down, minimizing, or somehow coping as a way to distract yourself from how you feel.
But eventually we do need to feel. Well, you don't need to. You can do what you like. It's your choice. But if you do nothing different, you probably know how it's going to go.

I'd recommend you do it when you're ready. And it often helps to feel in bits at a time instead of all at once, because there are layers to feeling. I'm not talking about the polyvagal state underneath. I mean there are just layers of feeling, and noticing one layer may lead to the next.
An easy example is anger. In therapy, and in life outside therapy, I have yet to work with anybody, or experience in myself, anger that was just about anger.

People tend to feel angry with other stuff underneath it. Anger is often driven by overwhelm, frustration, sadness, loneliness, shame, or guilt. What's seen day to day is anger or irritability, but there are other things under there. Rather than feeling those things, which maybe the person can't do yet, it comes across as anger. That's just the top layer.

This isn't because there's something wrong with you. We all do this. It's hard to feel our feelings sometimes, and that's okay. You're reading this, so you're open to something new, and to me that's a hell of a lot better than nothing. I applaud you for that.

Even if you really want to feel your feelings, it may still be difficult. You may not even see the issue. You may have no idea what's underneath your anger. Or you may be habitually thumbing through your phone, short videos or picture after picture, or shopping, and not realize you're doing it because there's something you're avoiding.
But no matter what, those feelings are there. Whether or not you feel them, they still affect you, and they're not really going anywhere.

Feeling them may not be easy right at this moment, but eventually I'd highly encourage you to work in the direction of feeling your feelings. You don't have to. But I think we both know they're not going anywhere. And if you don't feel them, I think that will keep you stuck, not just on an autonomic nervous system level, but in your potential in life: your potential to connect with others, and to find more life satisfaction, more calm, more happiness.
